lead: Sheet metal formability is the amount of strain a sheet can take before it necks or tears. A press forms a blank between a punch and a die; the useful shape is limited by how the metal hardens and how it resists thinning. Engineers judge it with the power law, the Lankford coefficient and the forming limit diagram. It decides whether a car panel, a steel cupboard door or a phone chassis can be pressed without splitting.
prereq: You need: true stress, true strain and plastic deformation from Unit 2: plastic deformation and yield criteria.

blocks.text: Every press operation starts with a blank: a flat sheet cut to the size that will be formed. The punch is the male tool that pushes the sheet; the die is the female tool with the opening or cavity. Clearance is the gap between punch and die at the cutting edge. In forming, the punch and die profile, the blank-holder force and friction set the strain path. Clearance matters mainly in cutting. A sheet that stretches too far thins, then necks first over a diffuse region and then in a narrow local band, and finally tears. That local neck is the failure to design against. Cutting clearance is covered in 3.2.

blocks.where: σ is true stress in MPa; K is the strength coefficient in MPa; ε is true strain (dimensionless); n is the strain-hardening exponent (dimensionless).

blocks.text: On a log-log plot the power law is a straight line of slope n. A higher n means the metal hardens more as it strains, so load spreads from a thin spot to its neighbours and necking is delayed. In a simple tensile test, diffuse necking starts near ε = n, so n is a rough stretchability index. It is not the whole story: a sheet can fail in a press at strains above or below n, because the strain path changes the limit. That is why the forming limit diagram is needed.

Normal anisotropy r compares the size of true width strain to the size of true thickness strain in a tensile test. In a tensile test the width and thickness both shrink, so their true strains are negative. r uses the magnitudes, so r is positive. A high r means the sheet strains more in width than in thickness, so it resists thinning. Deep-drawing steels often have r between 1.5 and 2.0; many aluminium sheets sit nearer 0.6 to 0.8. Thickness strain is hard to measure directly, so it is often found from volume constancy. Example: r = 1.8 means the width strain is 1.8 times the thickness strain in size.

blocks.where: ε<sub>width</sub> is true strain across the strip width; ε<sub>thickness</sub> is true strain through the sheet thickness; w<sub>0</sub> and w are initial and current width; t<sub>0</sub> and t are initial and current thickness; ln is the natural logarithm. r is positive and dimensionless. r is also called the Lankford coefficient.

blocks.text: r is not n. n measures how stress grows with strain; r measures the direction of strain. A high-n sheet resists necking. A high-r sheet resists thinning, which helps a cup draw without splitting. Some syllabi average r over 0°, 45° and 90° to the rolling direction and call it normal anisotropy; the variation with direction is planar anisotropy.

The forming limit diagram (FLD) plots major true strain ε1 on the vertical axis against minor true strain ε2 on the horizontal axis. ε1 is the larger principal strain at a point; ε2 is the smaller principal strain, with sign. The forming limit curve (FLC) separates safe strains below it from local necking above it. On the left, ε2 is negative: tension-compression, as in drawing a cup. On the right, ε2 is positive: tension-tension, as in stretching over a dome. The lowest point is near plane strain, ε2 = 0, where sheets are least tolerant. Deep drawing in 3.4 sits on the left; stretch forming in 3.5 sits on the right.

items: Find the critical points of the part, such as corners, domes and draw walls.
Measure or simulate the true major strain ε1 and minor strain ε2 at each point.
Plot each point as (ε2, ε1) on the FLD.
Keep the point below the FLC with a safety margin; above the curve means local necking is predicted.

blocks.text: The tensile test gives K, n and r from a strip, but not the whole FLD. The Erichsen cupping test presses a steel ball into a clamped sheet until a crack appears and reports cup depth in mm; a deeper cup means better stretch formability. A full FLD is built by testing specimens of different widths, each giving a different strain path.

figure.caption: Flow stress against true strain for the worked example. At ε = 0.20 the curve reads about 362 MPa, and n = 0.20 is also the tensile necking strain.

spec.aria: Plot of flow stress rising with true strain, following the power law with K equal to 500 megapascals and n equal to 0.20.

examples.question: A steel sheet follows σ = 500ε<sup>0.20</sup>, with σ in MPa. Find the true stress at ε = 0.20 and state what happens at that strain if necking begins when ε = n.
steps: List the data: K = 500 MPa, n = 0.20, ε = 0.20.
Apply the power law: σ = K ε<sup>n</sup> = 500 × 0.20<sup>0.20</sup>.
Necking begins when ε = n. Here n = 0.20, so ε = 0.20 is the necking strain.
examples.answer: The true stress is σ ≈ 362.4 MPa, and at ε = 0.20 the tensile test reaches necking because ε = n = 0.20.
examples.check:
K = 500.0
n = 0.20
eps = 0.20
sigma = K * eps**n
print(round(sigma, 1))

traps: Using engineering strain or tensile elongation as the only formability measure. The FLD needs true major and minor strains.
Swapping the FLD axes: ε1 (major) is vertical, ε2 (minor) is horizontal.
Treating n and r as the same. n is the strain-hardening exponent; r is the width-to-thickness strain ratio.
Forgetting that the safe side of the FLD is below the curve, and that plane strain near ε2 = 0 is the least tolerant path.
Reading a high n as a guarantee against tearing. The strain path and the local geometry also decide failure.

quiz.q: Define blank, punch and die in a sheet metal press operation.
quiz.a: Blank: flat sheet cut to the required outline. Punch: male tool that pushes or shears the sheet. Die: female tool with the opening or cavity that the punch works against.

quiz.q: Write the power law for sheet metal flow stress and name each term.
quiz.a: σ = Kε<sup>n</sup>, where σ is true stress in MPa, K is strength coefficient in MPa, ε is true strain and n is the strain-hardening exponent.

quiz.q: Why does a higher strain-hardening exponent n delay necking?
quiz.a: Higher n means flow stress rises faster with strain. A thin region that strains more becomes stronger, so load shifts to neighbouring regions and growth of the thin spot slows. In a simple tensile test diffuse necking starts near ε = n.

quiz.q: A steel sheet has r = 1.8. What does this say about thinning during forming?
quiz.a: For the same tensile strain, width strain is 1.8 times thickness strain. The sheet resists thinning, which helps drawability.

quiz.q: A sheet has K = 600 MPa and n = 0.22. Find the true stress at ε = 0.15.
At a point on a pressed panel, ε1 = 0.30 and ε2 = 0.10. The FLC at ε2 = 0.10 gives ε1 = 0.28. Is the point safe?
quiz.a: No. The point lies 0.02 above the FLC in major strain, so local necking is predicted.

quiz.q: Why is the lowest point of a forming limit curve near plane strain, ε2 = 0?
quiz.a: At ε<sub>2</sub> = 0 the sheet cannot spread sideways, so a locally thinner patch must take all its extra deformation as thickness reduction. Any width strain (positive or negative) lets the material flow in the plane and shares the deformation, so the limit strain is higher away from plane strain.

quiz.q: A corner of a drawn cup tears. Measured strains are high ε1 and ε2 near zero. Give two changes to the process or design.
quiz.a: Reduce local stretch by increasing the corner radius or improving the blank shape so more metal flows in. Reduce blank-holder force or add lubrication to lower the strain path. A sheet with higher n or r also helps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Press shops combine the FLD with finite-element simulation and grid marking or digital image correlation to see strains on real panels. Advanced high-strength steels and aluminium need anisotropic yield models and careful lubrication. Search for forming limit diagram, Lankford coefficient, Erichsen cupping test and sheet metal forming simulation.
